title: [Proxy] CONNECT tunnels are keyed by proxy and origin only, so tunnels authenticated with other credentials are reused
body:
## Summary
BuildConnectTunnelPoolKey and the HTTP/2 tunnel lookup use proxy host, port and target only, not ProxySettings.Credentials. UHttpClient shares HttpTransportFactory.Default across clients with default options regardless of options.Proxy, so a client with different or no proxy credentials reuses another client's authenticated tunnel. The proxy then attributes the traffic to the wrong user and rotated credentials keep being ignored on old tunnels.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:1368`

## Problem
BuildConnectTunnelPoolKey (1368-1378) is 'tunnel|proxyHost:port:|targetHost:port:s'. A reused tunnel is accepted when PoolKey matches (1232-1240) and the HTTP/2 fast path looks up (host, port, proxyHost, proxyPort) (868). Neither includes ProxySettings.Credentials. UHttpClient uses the shared HttpTransportFactory.Default whenever TlsBackend, ConnectionPool, Http2 and Streaming options are default (UHttpClient.cs:120-140), independent of options.Proxy, so clients with different proxy identities share one pool.

**Failure scenario.** Client A (proxy user alice) opens a tunnel to api.example through proxy P. Client B in the same process is configured for P with user bob, or with no credentials at all. B's request to api.example reuses A's idle tunnel: it passes the proxy without authenticating and the proxy attributes the traffic to alice. After credentials are rotated, old tunnels keep being used under the old identity.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 Section 11.7.2

## Suggested fix
Add a credential discriminator (for example a hash of user name and password, or an identity id of the ProxySettings instance) to the tunnel pool key and to the tunneled HTTP/2 manager key. Document the key in architecture.md.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The tunnel pool key and the tunnelled HTTP/2 manager key include a credential discriminator (hash of credentials or a ProxySettings identity)
- [ ] Clients with different or no proxy credentials never share an idle tunnel
- [ ] The key format is documented in architecture.md
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix with two clients using different proxy credentials against one proxy and origin

title: [Proxy] An interim 1xx reply to CONNECT is treated as the final reply and fails the tunnel
body:
## Summary
The CONNECT reply loop in RawSocketTransport evaluates the first response head it reads as the final reply. A 1xx interim response (other than 101) that precedes the real 2xx is therefore treated as a failed tunnel. RFC 9110 allows a server or proxy to send interim responses before the final one, so users behind such proxies cannot establish HTTPS tunnels.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:1512`

## Problem
EstablishConnectTunnelAsync reads one reply (1449), accepts 2xx (1453), handles 407 (1470-1510) and throws 'CONNECT tunnel failed with status N' for everything else (1512-1514). ConnectReplyReader.ParseStatusCode accepts any code >= 100 (ConnectReplyReader.cs:261-264) and ConnectReply.IsTunnelEstablished is 200-299 only, so a 1xx head ends the exchange. The HTTP/1.1 response parser has a 1xx loop with Max1xxResponses; the CONNECT path has none.

**Failure scenario.** A proxy (or an intermediary in front of it) sends 'HTTP/1.1 100 Continue' or a 103 before 'HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established': the client fails the request with NetworkError 'CONNECT tunnel failed with status 100' and closes a connection whose tunnel was about to open.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 Section 15.2

## Suggested fix
Skip 1xx heads (other than 101) in the CONNECT reply loop, bounded by the same Max1xxResponses limit and header budget, then evaluate the final reply.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] CONNECT reply parsing skips 1xx heads (other than 101) and evaluates the final reply, per RFC 9110 section 15.2
- [ ] The skip is bounded by the same Max1xxResponses limit and header budget used for normal responses; exceeding it fails with UHttpException
- [ ] A 1xx followed by 200 establishes the tunnel; a 1xx followed by 407 or 502 is reported as the final failure
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix

title: [HTTP/1.1] One-shot send path never reads the server's early final response when the request body write fails
body:
## Summary
When the request body write fails on the non-Expect path, the transport surfaces the send exception and never tries to read a response. A server that rejects early (for example 413 or 401) and closes the connection has already sent a final response, which is discarded. The Expect: 100-continue path already handles this case.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/RawSocketTransport.cs:1923`

## Problem
SendOnLeaseAsync (RawSocketTransport.cs:1923-1946) awaits Http11RequestSerializer.SerializeAsync for head and whole body and only then calls ParseHeadAsync. An IOException/SocketException from a body write propagates straight out (the finally at 1933 only records bytes sent); nothing attempts to read a response that is already in the receive buffer. DispatchAttemptAsync then either replays the request on a fresh connection (reused connection + idempotent, 665-669), maps it to 'Connection failed after a non-replayable request body started sending' (730-737), or to NetworkError (805-808). Only the Expect: 100-continue path captures the send failure and still reads the final head (TrySendRequestBodyAsync 2338-2364, ReadExpectContinueFinalHeadAsync 2190-2223, CompleteExpectContinueHead 2234-2264, which cites RFC 9112 9.5), and auto-Expect is off by default (StreamingOptions.AutoExpectContinueThresholdBytes is null, StreamingOptions.cs:27). The only test of the rule is the Expect path (RawSocketTransportConnectionReuseTests.ExpectContinue_BodySendFailure_ErrorFinalResponse_ReturnedAndConnectionNotReused).

**Failure scenario.** PUT/POST of a 50 MB body without Expect to a server that answers 413/401/403 after the headers and closes: the client's next body write fails with a reset, the caller gets UHttpErrorType.NetworkError (or, for an idempotent PUT on a reused connection, the whole upload is started again on a new connection and fails the same way) and never sees the status code or the error body the server sent.

## Spec reference
RFC 9112 Section 9.5

## Suggested fix
On a body-write failure in the one-shot path, do what the Expect path already does: keep the send exception, try to parse a final head from the connection (bounded by the request token), return a non-2xx head with KeepAlive=false, and only surface the send failure when no final response can be read. Also stop sending the body once a final head is available.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After a body-write failure on the one-shot path, the transport attempts to parse a final response head from the connection, bounded by the request token
- [ ] If a final head is read, it is returned as a normal non-2xx response with KeepAlive=false, and the connection is not reused
- [ ] Only when no final response can be read is the original send failure surfaced as UHttpException
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with a server that replies 413 and closes mid-body, failing before the fix

## Context

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. SendOnLeaseAsync (RawSocketTransport.cs:1923-1936) awaits Http11RequestSerializer.SerializeAsync for head+body; the finally only records bytes sent, and ParseHeadAsync (:1941/:1958) is reached only when the whole write succeeded. A write IOException/SocketException goes to the stale filter (:665-669; CanRetryHttp11RequestAfterTransportFailure :284-300 returns true for any idempotent replayable request, so a PUT on a reused connection is re-uploaded on GetNewConnectionAsync :683), to CreateCommittedNonReplayableBodyFailure (:730-737), or to NetworkError (:805-808). Only the Expect path keeps the send failure and still reads the final head (TrySendRequestBodyAsync :2338-2364, ReadExpectContinueFinalHeadAsync :2190-2223, CompleteExpectContinueHead :2234-2264), and auto-Expect is off unless AutoExpectContinueThresholdBytes is set (:420-422). No guard or test for the one-shot path found. RFC 9112 Section 9.5 is a SHOULD and an RST can discard the unread response on some stacks, so the fix is best effort, but the client never tries.

Also reported as `http1-protocol-01` (merged into this issue).

title: [Transport] PollSelect receives always take a poll-thread round trip and an extra copy, capped at 16 KB per read
body:
## Summary
PollSelectSocketChannel queues every receive to the poll thread and copies the data from an intermediate pooled buffer into the caller's array, with each read capped at 16 KB. Even when data is already available this costs a thread hop and a copy per read. This affects throughput and latency on platforms that use the PollSelect mode.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:159`

## Problem
SendAsync first tries a non-blocking send on the caller's thread (:192-215); ReceiveAsync has no such attempt and always parks the operation for the poll thread (:150-164), even when the kernel buffer already holds data, so each read costs a signal, a Poll syscall, the Receive and a cross-thread completion. The poll thread receives into _recvBuffer and then BlockCopies into the caller's buffer (:324, :337); unlike SAEA there is no in-flight kernel ownership to protect, since the copy into the caller's buffer happens on the same thread immediately afterwards. The count is capped to _recvBuffer.Length (:159). Each cancellable read also allocates a registration and a boxed async state machine (:171-172, :605-614), and the byte[] Stream overload adds AsTask (PollSelectStream.cs:52).

**Failure scenario.** Downloading a large body in PollSelect mode: every 16 KB costs two context switches, two copies and three allocations where a direct non-blocking Receive into the caller's buffer would cost one syscall when data is already buffered.

## Suggested fix
Try a non-blocking Receive straight into the caller's array on the calling thread first and queue for the poll thread only on WouldBlock; let the poll thread receive directly into the caller's array as well.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A receive first tries a non-blocking Socket.Receive directly into the caller's array on the calling thread and queues to the poll thread only on WouldBlock
- [ ] The poll thread receives directly into the caller's array, removing the intermediate copy and the 16 KB cap
- [ ] Measured: zero extra buffer copies per receive on the ready-data path and no poll-thread round trip, shown by a benchmark or counter
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ covering ready-data and WouldBlock paths and reads larger than 16 KB

title: [Transport] PollSelect ServiceRecv/ServiceSend complete the operation without re-checking that it is still pending
body:
## Summary
ServiceRecv and ServiceSend on the poll thread complete the pending operation without taking the guard that FailRecv and FailSend use to confirm it is still active. If cancellation or dispose already completed the operation, the poll thread can complete it a second time or write into a buffer the caller no longer owns. The race window is small but corrupts ownership of the pooled buffer and the completion source.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:345`

## Problem
ServiceRecv samples _recvPending under the lock (:312-319), then receives and copies into the caller's buffer outside it (:324-337), then unconditionally clears the flag and calls src.SetResult (:345-346). ServiceSend does the same (:382-389). AbandonPendingOperations, which any caller thread runs from PublishWork once _disposed is set (:506-514), takes the same flag and calls SetException on the same source (:483-504). When it runs between the sample and the completion, the source is completed twice: ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore throws InvalidOperationException on the poll thread, which escapes RunPollLoop as an unhandled thread exception, and the copy at :337 has written into a buffer whose operation the caller already saw fail (and may have returned to the pool).

**Failure scenario.** HTTP/2 over PollSelect: the connection is disposed while a receive is being serviced, and a writer calls SendAsync at the same moment; its PublishWork aborts the pending receive, then the poll thread completes it again. Result: an unhandled exception on the poll thread and a late write into the reader's buffer.

## Suggested fix
Complete under the same guard as FailRecv/FailSend: re-take the lock, return if the flag is already clear, clear it, then complete; do the copy only after winning that check.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ServiceRecv and ServiceSend re-take the lock, return if the pending flag is already clear, clear it, and only then copy and complete
- [ ] The copy into the caller's array happens only after the pending check has been won
- [ ] A cancellation or dispose racing with a ready socket completes the operation exactly once
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that forces the race and fails before the fix

title: [Transport] PollSelectSocketChannel.Dispose joins its own poll thread from an I/O continuation, stalling 500 ms and abandoning both pooled buffers
body:
## Summary
When a continuation that runs on the poll thread disposes the channel (every non-keep-alive completion), Dispose calls Join on the thread it is running on. The join waits its full 500 ms timeout and then abandons both pooled buffers instead of returning them. Each non-keep-alive request on PollSelect platforms pays the stall and leaks two buffers from the pool.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:535`

## Problem
ReceiveAsync never completes inline (PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:146-173 always queues to the poll thread), and the poll thread completes the operation with src.SetResult/SetException (:346, :389, :463). PollSelectSource wraps ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<int> with RunContinuationsAsynchronously left false (:642), and every await in the transport is ConfigureAwait(false), so the whole continuation chain (WrapWithCancellationCleanup :605, PollSelectStream.ReadAsync(...).AsTask() PollSelectStream.cs:52, BufferedStreamReader, Http11ResponseBodySource, the handler) runs on the poll thread, inside ServiceRecv inside RunPollLoop. When that chain disposes the connection - Http11ResponseBodySource.CompleteBody -> _lease.Dispose() for a response without keep-alive (Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:673), CloseBody (:683), the stale-retry lease.Dispose() in RawSocketTransport.cs:671, any parse error - PooledConnection.Dispose -> PollSelectStream.Dispose -> PollSelectSocketChannel.Dispose runs on the poll thread and executes _pollThread.Join(500) (:535) on itself. There is no Thread.CurrentThread check. Join(self) cannot succeed, so it returns after 500 ms, IsAlive is true and both 16 KB buffers go to ByteArrayPool.Abandon (:542-546). No test disposes a channel from a continuation (Tests/Runtime/Transport/PollSelectSocketChannelTests.cs, SocketChannelLifecycleTests.cs).

**Failure scenario.** SocketIoMode.PollSelect, HTTP/1.1 server that answers 'Connection: close' (or HTTP/1.0, or a close-delimited body): the last body read is completed by the poll thread, CompleteBody disposes the lease on that thread, and the response reaches the caller 500 ms late; 32 KB of pooled buffers are dropped per connection. The same stall hits every error path that disposes the lease from a read continuation (malformed response, stale-connection retry before its fresh dial) and an HTTP/2 connection torn down by its read loop.

## Suggested fix
In Dispose, skip the Join when Thread.CurrentThread == _pollThread (the loop exits right after the continuation returns; hand the buffer return to the loop's finally), or set RunContinuationsAsynchronously on the sources so user continuations never run on the poll thread. Add a test that disposes the stream from a read continuation and asserts it returns promptly with the buffers returned.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dispose skips the Join when Thread.CurrentThread is the poll thread and the loop's finally block returns the buffers, or continuations never run on the poll thread (RunContinuationsAsynchronously)
- [ ] Disposing from a continuation on the poll thread returns immediately and both pooled buffers are returned exactly once
- [ ] Disposing from other threads keeps its bounded join and existing buffer-abandon behaviour when the join times out
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that disposes the channel from a poll-thread continuation and asserts no stall and buffers returned; fails before the fix

## Context

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. ReceiveAsync always queues to the poll thread (PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:146-173); ServiceRecv calls src.SetResult on that thread (:346). PollSelectSource wraps ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<int> with RunContinuationsAsynchronously left false (:640-660), and every await above it is ConfigureAwait(false) (WrapWithCancellationCleanup :605-614, PollSelectStream.ReadAsync .AsTask() PollSelectStream.cs:48-53, AbandonOnCancel's Task.WhenAny, BufferedStreamReader), so the chain runs inline on the poll thread; the poll thread has no SynchronizationContext. Http11ResponseBodySource.CompleteBody calls _lease.Dispose() for a non-keep-alive response (Http11ResponseBodySource.cs:660-673), then PooledConnection.Dispose (TcpConnectionPool.cs:139-144), PollSelectStream.Dispose (PollSelectStream.cs:118-125) and PollSelectSocketChannel.Dispose, which runs _pollThread.Join(500) (:535) with no Thread.CurrentThread check. Joining the current thread can only time out, so the continuation stalls 500 ms, IsAlive is true and both buffers go to ByteArrayPool.Abandon (:542-546). No test disposes the channel from a continuation (PollSelectSocketChannelTests, SocketChannelLifecycleTests). PollSelect is opt-in (default NetworkStream, ConnectionPoolOptions.cs:62) but is the mode the docs recommend for console/mobile IL2CPP (:32-45). Related hazard on the same thread: a TLS stream's close_notify on Dispose goes through the sync Write (GetAwaiter().GetResult(), PollSelectStream.cs:87-88) and would deadlock if the kernel buffer were full.

title: [Transport] SAEA and PollSelect channels and their Stream adapters are near-copies with no shared abstraction and diverging behaviour
body:
## Summary
SaeaSocketChannel, PollSelectSocketChannel and their stream adapters duplicate most of their logic. The copies already disagree on reads into non-array Memory and on how cancellation closes the socket, so fixes land in one and not the other. This raises the cost and risk of every transport change.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/PollSelectStream.cs:63`

## Problem
SaeaStream.cs (140 lines) and PollSelectStream.cs (136 lines) are the same file with the channel type swapped, but SaeaStream.ReadAsync(Memory) asks the channel for buffer.Length bytes (SaeaStream.cs:68) while PollSelectStream asks for tmp.Length (PollSelectStream.cs:63), where tmp comes from ByteArrayPool.Rent(buffer.Length) and ArrayPool may return a larger array; CopyAndReturnPooledAsync then copies n bytes into a shorter destination. Tests/Runtime/Transport/TcpStreamAdapterTests.cs:56 sizes the destination to the exact payload, so the over-read is never exercised. The two channels duplicate ThrowIfCancelledOrDisposed (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:389-394, PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:560-565), the cancellation-race predicate under two names (IsCancellationRace 402-403 vs IsLostToCancellation 627-628) and four copies of the 'ct.Register(static s => ((Socket)s).Dispose())' callback (Saea 170-173 and 241-244, PollSelect 171 and 231). That callback closes the descriptor directly, while SaeaSocketChannel.Dispose (328-340), SocketHandleHold.Close (235) and RawSocketTransport.RegisterDisposeOnCancel (322) all shut down first for the #384 reason spelled out in the Dispose comment; registrations run last-registered-first, so the channel's direct close runs before the transport's shutdown. Both adapters also keep sync Read/Write overrides implemented as GetAwaiter().GetResult() (baselined RS0030) that no pipeline component calls.

**Failure scenario.** PollSelect mode with a caller that reads into a MemoryManager-backed Memory<byte> of 100 bytes while 4 KB are pending: the channel reads up to the rented array's length, CopyTo throws ArgumentException and the bytes are gone from the stream. SAEA mode on an IL2CPP selector platform: a request cancel or an HTTP/2 connection shutdown fires the channel registration first and closes the descriptor under the pending receive, the exact order #384 forbids (device confirmation needed).

## Suggested fix
Introduce one internal ISocketChannel (ReceiveAsync/SendAsync/Dispose) with a single SocketChannelStream adapter, and one shared cancellation helper that performs the shutdown-first close through the channel's own Dispose logic instead of Socket.Dispose. Make the sync overrides throw NotSupportedException or remove them from the baseline by deleting them.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One internal ISocketChannel (ReceiveAsync, SendAsync, Dispose) and a single SocketChannelStream adapter replace the duplicated adapters
- [ ] One shared cancellation helper performs the shutdown-first close through the channel's own Dispose logic instead of Socket.Dispose
- [ ] Synchronous Stream overrides throw NotSupportedException consistently in both modes
- [ ] Existing channel tests run against both implementations in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ and pass unchanged

## Context

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Mostly confirmed, with one sub-claim wrong and one device-dependent. Duplication is real: the two adapters are the same file with the channel type swapped, and the channels repeat ThrowIfCancelledOrDisposed (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:389-394, PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:560-565), the cancellation-race predicate under two names (:402-403 vs :627-628) and the Socket.Dispose registration four times. The over-read is real but latent: PollSelectStream passes tmp.Length (PollSelectStream.cs:63) where SaeaStream passes buffer.Length (SaeaStream.cs:68); ByteArrayPool.Rent is ArrayPool.Shared (ByteArrayPool.cs:56, :73) and may return a larger array, the channel reads up to Min(count, _recvBuffer.Length), and CopyTo into the shorter destination then throws after the bytes were consumed. No library reader passes non-array memory (the parsers and the frame codec use the byte[] overload), and TcpStreamAdapterTests.cs:56-58 sizes the owner to the exact payload, so only an external caller of the stream can hit it. The #384 sub-claim is plausible only: the SAEA registration closes the descriptor directly (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:170-173, :241-244) while Dispose shuts down first on selector platforms (:328-340); registrations on one token run last-registered-first, so on cancel the direct close precedes the transport's shutdown (RawSocketTransport.cs:319-324). Whether that loses a later receive on IL2CPP needs a device run, and SAEA is opt-in. Wrong sub-claim: the sync Read/Write overrides are not provably unused, BouncyCastleTlsStream calls _inner.Read and _inner.Write (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:184, :506), so making them throw is not a safe recommendation.

title: [Transport] PollSelectStream.ReadAsync(Memory) requests the rented array's length instead of the destination's length
body:
## Summary
ReadAsync(Memory<byte>) in PollSelectStream passes the length of the rented intermediate array as the receive count instead of the destination buffer's length. The receive can return more bytes than the destination holds, which are truncated or mishandled. Callers using small destination buffers can lose data.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/PollSelectStream.cs:63`

## Problem
For a Memory<byte> that is not array-backed the stream rents tmp = ByteArrayPool.Rent(buffer.Length) and calls _channel.ReceiveAsync(tmp, 0, tmp.Length, ...) (:62-63). ArrayPool rounds up (ByteArrayPool.cs:64-66: 'The returned array may be larger than requested'), so the channel may deliver more bytes than the destination holds; CopyAndReturnPooledAsync then does tmp.AsMemory(0, n).CopyTo(destination) (:74-75), which throws ArgumentException, and the bytes already taken from the socket are lost. SaeaStream passes buffer.Length correctly (SaeaStream.cs:68). The existing test sends exactly as many bytes as the destination holds, so it cannot see this (TcpStreamAdapterTests.cs:52-58).

**Failure scenario.** A caller reads into a 100-byte native-memory-backed Memory<byte> while 128 or more bytes are buffered: Rent(100) returns a 128-byte array, 128 bytes are received, the copy throws and the stream has silently dropped data.

## Suggested fix
Pass buffer.Length as the count, and extend the test with a payload larger than the destination.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ReadAsync passes buffer.Length as the receive count and never returns more bytes than the destination can hold
- [ ] No bytes are lost or duplicated when the available payload exceeds the destination length
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with a payload larger than the destination buffer, failing before the fix

title: [Transport] Close order is chosen from a compile-time 'IOCP' label for Windows, but Mono and IL2CPP do not use IOCP for Socket I/O
body:
## Summary
SaeaPlatformDetection labels Windows as IOCP and picks the close-first order with no descriptor hold. Neither Mono nor IL2CPP uses IOCP for Socket I/O, so Windows IL2CPP players get close-first without the stale-selector-job protection that other IL2CPP platforms get. The documentation also describes Windows as IOCP.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaPlatformDetection.cs:72`

## Problem
CompletionModelName returns "IOCP" for UNITY_EDITOR_WIN || UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN (SaeaPlatformDetection.cs:51-52) and CloseAbortsPendingIo is CompletionModelName == "IOCP" (:72). That switches off the hold (SocketHandleHold.cs:64, s_holdsPendingIo = 0) and selects close-first in SaeaSocketChannel (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:53, :318-325, comment 'IOCP has no descriptor-keyed selector to go stale'). On Unity's runtimes Socket async I/O (BeginReceive/ReceiveAsync, which NetworkStream and SAEA both use) goes through the class library's IOSelector, i.e. the runtime's threadpool I/O selector with a poll backend on Windows as well; there is no IOCP path. SocketHandleHold's own comment says the stale job comes from libil2cpp's Socket::Close_icall not removing the job from that selector (SocketHandleHold.cs:15-21), which is platform-independent libil2cpp code. The Windows decision appears to rest on Mono behaviour (Mono's Socket.Dispose removes the job); a Windows IL2CPP standalone player is a supported target and gets neither the hold nor shutdown-first.

**Failure scenario.** Windows standalone IL2CPP build, NetworkStream mode: a first-byte timeout or request timeout abandons a pending read and the socket handle is closed at once; the retry socket is given the recycled SOCKET handle value, its receive is queued behind the stale selector job and the retry stalls to its first-byte bound or the request timeout. Confirm by running ReusedConnectionFirstByteTimeoutTests / the Loop384 loop on a Windows IL2CPP player and logging SocketHandleHold.HoldsPendingIo.

## Suggested fix
Decide the close order from what was measured per runtime, not from an OS label: validate Windows IL2CPP explicitly (does shutdown end a pending receive there, does close leave the job), and record it; until then do not describe Windows as IOCP in the detection or the SocketIoMode docs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The close order is decided from what was measured per runtime, not from an OS label
- [ ] Windows IL2CPP behaviour (does shutdown end a pending receive, does close leave a stale job) is validated on a Windows IL2CPP player and recorded
- [ ] Detection code and SocketIoMode docs no longer describe Windows as IOCP unless measured
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ for the detection decision per runtime/platform input

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `net-runtime-04` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/net.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: platform-compat.

Verification: Plausible: the code is as described; the outcome depends on runtime, device or peer behaviour that a static review cannot settle.

Verifier note: Code as described: CompletionModelName is 'IOCP' for UNITY_EDITOR_WIN || UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN (SaeaPlatformDetection.cs:51-52), CloseAbortsPendingIo derives from that string (:72), and it switches off the hold (SocketHandleHold.cs:64) and selects close-first in the SAEA channel (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:53, :318-325). The Windows decision was measured, but only on the Windows Editor (Mono): PR #405 records that a hold there kept the abandoned read for the full bound and failed RawSocketTransportCancellationTests, and states verbatim 'Windows IL2CPP Standalone keeps the close-first order and is unvalidated for the stale-job case'. So the gap is acknowledged in a merged PR body but no open issue tracks it (#384 is iOS/selector scoped, #99 is iOS+Android, #404 standalone rows are generic). Whether libil2cpp on Windows leaves a handle-keyed job after close, and whether Windows recycles the SOCKET value quickly enough to hit it, cannot be settled statically. The 'IOCP' wording in the detection and in ConnectionPoolOptions.cs:21/:197 is inaccurate for Mono/IL2CPP socket I/O, but that part is documentation, not behaviour.

title: [Transport] Shipping socket channel types carry test-only hooks and process-wide static switches that tests mutate
body:
## Summary
SaeaSocketChannel and related types expose Action hooks and mutable static switches used only by tests. Tests that change process-wide statics can interfere with each other, and production types carry test scaffolding. This is a maintainability and test-isolation problem.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaSocketChannel.cs:122`

## Problem
SaeaSocketChannel: TestHookBeforeRegister (102), TestHookReceiveEnded invoked on every receive completion (110, 278), SetDrainTimeoutForTest (129), SimulateStuckReceiveForTest, which writes _recvActive (135-139), and the static settable ShutdownBeforeClose that changes the close order for every channel in the process (122-126). PollSelectSocketChannel: TestHookBeforeRegister, TestHookSendFailing, TestHookReceiveFailing as unsynchronised Action properties read on the caller and poll threads (128-138, 170, 203, 453, 468) and PollIterations incremented with Interlocked on every loop turn (247). SocketHandleHold: static settable HoldTimeout and HoldsPendingIo (101-117). TcpConnectionPool has two internal test constructors that cannot be combined (384-405). Tests/Runtime/Transport/SaeaShutdownOrderTests.cs:34 restores ShutdownBeforeClose in TearDown, i.e. a failed or aborted test leaves the process-wide close order flipped.

**Failure scenario.** A test that flips SaeaSocketChannel.ShutdownBeforeClose or SocketHandleHold.HoldsPendingIo and is interrupted (Editor domain kept alive, play mode without domain reload) leaves every later connection in the Editor session using the non-platform close order, which is exactly the configuration #384 documents as losing receives; the hooks also make the production types' real invariants (who may write _recvActive) harder to state.

## Suggested fix
Inject the close-order policy and timeouts through an internal options object passed to the constructor (tests build their own), replace the Action hooks with an internal observer interface that is null in production, and keep statics read-only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Close-order policy and timeouts are injected through an internal options object passed to the constructor; tests build their own
- [ ] Test Action hooks are replaced by an internal observer interface that is null in production
- [ ] No static field read by production code is mutated by tests; statics are readonly
- [ ] Existing transport tests in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ are migrated and pass without static resets

title: [Transport] SAEA mode allocates per pending operation and copies every byte twice, contrary to its documented allocation saving
body:
## Summary
The SAEA channel wraps each pending operation in an async method and receives into an intermediate pinned buffer before copying into the caller's buffer. Every operation allocates and every byte is copied twice, so SAEA mode does not deliver the allocation saving it is documented for.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaSocketChannel.cs:149`

## Problem
ReceiveAsync and SendAsync are async ValueTask methods (:149, :216): whenever the socket operation is pending (the normal case for a receive) the state machine is boxed, and each call makes a CancellationTokenRegistration (:170, :241). All readers in the transport call the byte[] overload (Http11ResponseParser.cs:1379 and :1415, Http2FrameCodec.cs:260), which SaeaStream implements as _channel.ReceiveAsync(...).AsTask() (SaeaStream.cs:52-57), a Task per pending read on top. Received bytes are copied kernel -> _recvBuffer -> caller buffer (:190) and sent bytes caller -> _sendBuffer -> kernel (:232), with one socket call per 16 KB chunk in both directions (BufferSize :43, :159, :231). The public docs promise the opposite: 'avoiding per-operation Task allocations on the hot receive path' (ConnectionPoolOptions.cs:17-23) and 'zero-allocation send and receive' (class summary :10-11).

**Failure scenario.** A project switches to SocketIoMode.Saea to cut GC on downloads: each pending read now costs a boxed state machine, a Task and a registration plus a 16 KB memcpy, and a 1 MB upload takes at least 64 copy+send round trips. Measured allocation per read is likely no better than NetworkStream mode (compare with the frame counter of #426/#434).

## Suggested fix
Return the IValueTaskSource directly from non-async methods (register cancellation in the source, as BufferedStreamReader does for body reads), have the hot readers call the Memory overloads, and receive straight into array-backed caller buffers on selector platforms, where the pinned intermediate buffer buys nothing. Otherwise correct the documentation.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Non-async methods return the IValueTaskSource directly, with cancellation registered in the source
- [ ] Hot readers call the Memory overloads, and array-backed caller buffers are received into directly on selector platforms
- [ ] Measured target: zero managed allocations per pending operation in steady state and one copy fewer per read, shown by an allocation test or benchmark
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ asserting allocation count on the read and write paths

The hot readers use the byte[] overload (Http11ResponseParser.cs:1379 and :1415, Http2FrameCodec.cs:260), which SaeaStream maps to ReceiveAsync(...).AsTask() (SaeaStream.cs:52-57). title: [Transport] Token cancellation in SAEA and PollSelect channels closes the socket directly, bypassing the shutdown-first order used by Dispose
body:
## Summary
The cancellation callback disposes the socket directly instead of using the shutdown-first sequence that Dispose uses to avoid the IL2CPP stale-selector-job hazard. A cancelled read can therefore leave a stale job on a descriptor that is then reused, which can lose the next socket's first receive.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaSocketChannel.cs:170`

## Problem
SaeaSocketChannel.Dispose shuts down, drains and only then closes on selector platforms, with the stated reason 'IL2CPP's close does not remove a pending job from its selector, so closing first would let a new socket reuse the number behind the stale job (#384)' (:326-341). But each operation registers its own cancellation callback that calls Socket.Dispose() directly (ReceiveAsync :170-173, SendAsync :241-244; PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:171 and :231 do the same). That callback is registered per read, i.e. after RawSocketTransport.RegisterDisposeOnCancel (RawSocketTransport.cs:1776, :319-324, which does Shutdown then Dispose), and CancellationTokenSource runs callbacks last-registered-first, so on a request timeout the channel's close-first callback normally runs before the shutdown-first one. In the body phase, the TLS handshake and the HTTP/2 read loop there is no RegisterDisposeOnCancel at all, so close-first is the only path. Afterwards the channel is still not disposed and _recvActive stays 1 if the completion is never posted, so the later Dispose spins 2 x 500 ms (:337-340) and abandons the buffers. #384's open remainder for SAEA mentions only the 500 ms fallback inside Dispose, not this path.

**Failure scenario.** SocketIoMode.Saea on an iOS/Android IL2CPP player: a request times out while its header or body read is pending. The channel's registration closes the descriptor under the pending receive job; the retry (or any new connection) gets the same descriptor number, queues its receive behind the stale job and loses it, which is the #364/#384 symptom the hold was built to remove; the thread that later disposes the channel blocks up to 1 s. Confirm with the Loop384 scenario run in SAEA mode on the iOS simulator or a device.

## Suggested fix
Route cancellation through the same sequence as Dispose: the registration should only Shutdown(Both) the socket (which ends the pending operation with the descriptor still open) and leave the close to the channel's Dispose, or call a non-blocking 'begin dispose' that defers the close until the in-flight flags clear.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Cancellation only calls Shutdown(Both) (ending the pending operation with the descriptor still open) and leaves the close to the channel's Dispose, or calls a non-blocking begin-dispose that defers the close
- [ ] Cancelled operations complete with the cancellation error and the descriptor is released only after the operation has ended
- [ ] Behaviour is validated on an IL2CPP device or simulator and recorded
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that observes the close sequence on cancellation and fails before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `net-runtime-03` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/net.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: platform-compat.

Verification: Plausible: the code is as described; the outcome depends on runtime, device or peer behaviour that a static review cannot settle.

Verifier note: Code as described for SAEA: the per-operation registration calls Socket.Dispose() directly (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:170-173, :241-244), while Dispose uses shutdown, drain, close on selector platforms for the stated #384 reason (:326-341). The transport passes the request token into the stream read (Http11ResponseParser.cs:1379), so the registration is live in the head phase; in the body phase, the TLS handshake and the HTTP/2 read loop no RegisterDisposeOnCancel exists at all. Head-phase order is not guaranteed either way (CancellationTokenSource runs callbacks last-registered-first only within one registration list), and when RegisterDisposeOnCancel (:319-324) runs first the channel's own Dispose does shutdown-first, so the close-first outcome there is timing dependent. The first-byte watchdog path is fine: RegisterDisposeOnCancel is registered on watchdog.Token after the linked source (:1987-1992), so it runs before the linked token reaches the channel. Whether close-first leaves a stale selector job and loses a later receive is IL2CPP device behaviour (needs-device-validation). #384 is open and covers 'no socket is created on a descriptor whose abandoned read has not ended'; its recorded SAEA remainder names only the 500 ms fallback inside Dispose, so this token path is an unlisted instance. The PollSelect half of the title does not hold for the selector hazard: PollSelect runs synchronous calls on its own thread and puts no job in the runtime selector (PR #405 notes), though its registration (PollSelectSocketChannel.cs:171, :231) does close the descriptor under the poll thread.

Related: #162, #364, #384, [[R11-net-design-09]], [[R11-net-runtime-13]], [[R11-net-runtime-04]].

title: [Transport] SaeaSocketChannel reads and writes its pooled buffers after Dispose may have returned them to ByteArrayPool
body:
## Summary
The channel clears its active flags before copying from the pooled buffer into the caller's buffer, and does not re-check the disposed state after taking an active flag. Dispose can therefore return the buffers to ByteArrayPool while a completion is still reading or writing them, which can corrupt another request's data from the pool.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaSocketChannel.cs:281`

## Problem
Receive: OnRecvCompleted clears _recvActive (:281) before ResolveFromSaea (:282); the awaiting ReceiveAsync then copies out of _recvBuffer (:189-190). The synchronous-completion path does the same (:183-190). Dispose only waits for _recvActive/_sendActive to be 0 (WaitForInFlightOperations :369-381) and then returns both buffers (:364-365). A Dispose on another thread that observes the flag between :281 and the BlockCopy returns _recvBuffer to the shared pool; the copy then delivers whatever the next renter wrote as this connection's bytes, with bytesRead > 0. Send: the chunk loop (:223-271) re-checks only the token (:225), takes _sendActive (:227) and copies caller data into _sendBuffer (:232) with no _disposed check; ThrowIfCancelledOrDisposed runs once before the loop (:218). A Dispose that completes between two chunks (or between :218 and :227) has already returned _sendBuffer, so :232 writes up to 16 KB of request bytes into a buffer another renter may own before _socket.SendAsync throws ObjectDisposedException. architecture.md lists this contract explicitly ('Never return a buffer while ... another thread may still touch it (SAEA in-flight flags ...)').

**Failure scenario.** SAEA mode, HTTP/2 upload: a DATA frame larger than 16 KB is being sent in chunks while the read loop hits a connection error and disposes the stream (not token-driven, so :225 does not stop the writer). Dispose sees _sendActive == 0 between chunks and returns _sendBuffer; a concurrent request rents it as its serializer buffer; the writer's next chunk overwrites it and that other request sends corrupted bytes (bytes of the first request) to a different server. Receive side: a timeout disposes the connection exactly as a body chunk completes and a streaming handler is handed bytes that belong to another connection before the cancellation surfaces.

## Suggested fix
Make the active flag cover the buffer use: copy into the caller's buffer in the completion path before clearing _recvActive (or clear it only after the copy), and after taking _sendActive/_recvActive re-check _disposed and bail out before touching the buffer, so Dispose's wait really excludes every buffer access.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The completion path copies into the caller's buffer before clearing the active flag, or clears it only after the copy
- [ ] After taking _sendActive or _recvActive the channel re-checks _disposed and bails out before touching a buffer
- [ ] Dispose's wait excludes every use of the pooled buffers, and buffers are returned exactly once
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ racing Dispose against completion and failing before the fix

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `net-runtime-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/net.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: resource-management.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: The code is as described and the flags do not cover the buffer use. Receive: OnRecvCompleted clears _recvActive (SaeaSocketChannel.cs:281) before ResolveFromSaea (:282) and the copy out of _recvBuffer happens in the awaiter afterwards (:187-190); the sync path clears at :183 before the copy. Send: the loop checks only the token (:225), takes _sendActive (:227) and copies into _sendBuffer (:232) with no _disposed re-check; ThrowIfCancelledOrDisposed runs once (:218). Dispose waits only for both flags to be 0 (:369-381) and then returns both buffers (:364-365). So a Dispose from another thread (RegisterDisposeOnCancel at a timeout, an HTTP/2 read-loop teardown) can return a buffer that the I/O continuation is about to read or the sender is about to fill. Downgraded because the window is nanoseconds wide and corruption additionally needs the buffer to be re-rented and written inside it: after the flag clears, the copy follows within the same continuation, while Dispose still has to close the socket and dispose two SAEAs before Return. In practice it needs a thread preemption at exactly that point. After Shutdown the next SendAsync fails and ends the loop, so there is no repeated exposure per send. SAEA is opt-in. Real invariant violation (journal 2026-02-phase19a.4 B-1 claims the flags make this safe), cheap to fix, low probability.

Related: [[R11-net-runtime-13]], [[R11-net-runtime-15]].

title: [Transport] SaeaSocketChannel.Dispose can block its caller for up to 1 s (two 500 ms drains), including inside cancellation callbacks
body:
## Summary
Dispose drains the receive and send operations one after the other, each with its own 500 ms wait, so a caller can block for up to a second. Dispose is also reached from cancellation callbacks, which then stall the cancelling thread and the timeout path.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/SaeaSocketChannel.cs:337`

## Problem
On selector platforms Dispose waits up to _drainTimeoutMs after the shutdown (:337) and again after the close when the first wait failed (:338-340), i.e. 2 x 500 ms of SpinWait on the disposing thread, which is the timer/caller thread when RawSocketTransport.RegisterDisposeOnCancel runs (RawSocketTransport.cs:319-324) and the main thread for a user-initiated Cancel or client.Dispose. The once-logged message reports 500 ms (:353-356). #168 tracks the bound itself.

**Failure scenario.** IL2CPP player, SAEA mode, completion never posted (the ~9% case measured in #384): each cancelled request blocks the cancelling thread for a full second before the buffers are abandoned.

## Suggested fix
Share one deadline across both drains and never wait inside the cancellation callback (defer the drain and buffer return to a completion-driven path).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The two drains share one deadline so Dispose blocks no more than a single bound
- [ ] Cancellation callbacks never wait; the drain and the buffer return are deferred to a completion-driven path
- [ ] Buffers are still not returned to the pool while the OS may write into them
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ using a fake socket whose operations never complete, asserting the bound and that cancellation does not block

title: [Transport] An undisposed TcpConnectionPool is kept alive forever by its scavenger loop
body:
## Summary
The pool's scavenger loop holds a strong reference to the pool, so a pool that is never disposed is never collected, along with its idle connections. Abandoned clients or pools in long-running apps leak sockets and memory. The scavenger also runs when no idle connection exists.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:375`

## Problem
The constructor starts RunIdleScavengerAsync with Task.Run (:374-375); the loop awaits Task.Delay(_scavengeInterval, ct) forever (:856-860) and its state machine captures this, so the timer queue roots the pool, its semaphores and its dictionaries until Dispose cancels _scavengeCts (:921-935). There is no finalizer or weak reference, and the loop keeps firing every 5-60 s (22.5 s with the mobile idle timeout) even when no connection is idle. In PollSelect mode each idle connection also keeps a thread.

**Failure scenario.** A project creates a UHttpClient with its own pool options per feature and does not dispose it (or the Editor exits play mode without domain reload with such clients alive): each leaked pool stays reachable and wakes a thread-pool thread periodically for the rest of the process.

## Suggested fix
Let the scavenger hold the pool through a WeakReference and stop when it is collected, and arm the timer only while at least one idle connection exists.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The scavenger holds the pool through a WeakReference and stops when the pool is collected
- [ ] The scavenger timer is armed only while at least one idle connection exists
- [ ] An undisposed, unreferenced pool becomes collectable and its scavenger stops
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test in Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that drops a pool and asserts the scavenger exits, failing before the fix

title: [Transport] TcpConnectionPool, ConnectionLease, PooledConnection and HappyEyeballsConnector are public and expose ownership-sensitive members
body:
## Summary
The connection pool types and the Happy Eyeballs connector are public, together with members that hand out pooled connections and leases. Callers can break the single-owner rules for pooled connections, and the pool defaults are duplicated outside ConnectionPoolOptions. Who owns the pool (the transport) is not documented. This becomes permanent public API once released.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:417`

## Problem
Public and reachable from user code: PooledConnection with its Socket and Stream properties and a public constructor (18-103); ConnectionLease.TransferOwnership/ReturnToPool (176-221), whose misuse double-owns or leaks a connection; TcpConnectionPool.GetConnectionAsync(host, port, secure, poolKeyOverride, ct) (417-425, no XML doc), which lets a caller file a connection under an arbitrary pool key such as another origin's tunnel key; HappyEyeballsConnector.ConnectAsync with a test-seam 'connector' parameter (Runtime/Transport/Connection/HappyEyeballsConnector.cs:56-62). None of them is used by Samples~ or Documentation~ (only 'new RawSocketTransport()' is). RawSocketTransport's public constructors take a caller-built pool (42-59) and Dispose() disposes it (2431) without saying ownership transfers, so two transports given one pool break each other on the first Dispose. Defaults exist in two places: TcpConnectionPool's constructor default maxConnectionsPerHost = 6 and DefaultDnsTimeoutMs = 10000 (271, 321) versus ConnectionPoolOptions (PlatformConfig.RecommendedMaxConcurrency, 10000), and Registration.WithOptions copies eight properties by hand (RawSocketTransport.cs:107-121), so a new pool option needs three coordinated edits.

**Failure scenario.** A user shares one TcpConnectionPool between two RawSocketTransport instances to share connections; disposing the first client disposes the pool and the second starts failing with ObjectDisposedException. After 1.0 these types cannot be changed (for example to merge the socket channels or move TLS wrapping into the pool) without a breaking change.

## Suggested fix
Make PooledConnection, ConnectionLease, the poolKeyOverride overload and HappyEyeballsConnector internal before the API freeze, give TcpConnectionPool a constructor that takes ConnectionPoolOptions (single source of defaults), and either document that the transport owns the pool or add a disposePool flag.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] PooledConnection, ConnectionLease, the poolKeyOverride overload and HappyEyeballsConnector are internal
- [ ] TcpConnectionPool has a constructor taking ConnectionPoolOptions so defaults come from one place
- [ ] XML docs state that the transport owns and disposes the pool (or a disposePool option exists)
- [ ] No test or sample depends on the removed public surface; Tests/Runtime/Transport/ compiles and passes

title: [Transport] HTTP/1.1 requests through one proxy share a single per-host permit set, so all origins compete for MaxConnectionsPerHost
body:
## Summary
Tunneled and proxied HTTP/1.1 connections take their per-host permit keyed by the proxy endpoint. Every origin behind the same proxy therefore shares MaxConnectionsPerHost connections. One busy origin can starve the others.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:451`

## Problem
GetConnectionCoreAsync builds the semaphore key from (host, port, secure) of the socket endpoint (451) and only the idle-queue key from poolKeyOverride (452-454). AcquirePreparedProxyLeaseAsync always passes the proxy host and port with secure: false (RawSocketTransport.cs:1218-1223), for forwarded http requests and for every CONNECT tunnel regardless of origin. The lease holds the permit for the whole HTTP/1.1 exchange, including a streamed response body.

**Failure scenario.** Behind a corporate proxy with the default limit of 6: six long downloads or long-poll requests to six different HTTPS origins occupy all permits; a request to a seventh origin waits in semaphore.WaitAsync until one finishes or its own timeout expires. Without the proxy each origin would have its own six.

## Suggested fix
Key the permit for tunneled connections by the tunnel pool key (origin x proxy) and give the proxy endpoint a separate, larger cap (browsers use 32 per proxy).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Permits for tunneled connections are keyed by the tunnel pool key (origin x proxy)
- [ ] The proxy endpoint has its own separate, larger cap (documented value)
- [ ] Direct connections keep the current per-host cap
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Transport] TcpConnectionPool idle queue is FIFO so the longest-idle connection is reused first and never ages out under load
body:
## Summary
The idle pool is a FIFO queue, so a request takes the connection that has been idle longest. That connection is the most likely to have been closed by the server or a middlebox, and it keeps all other idle connections alive so the scavenger never evicts them. The result is more reuse failures, retries and idle sockets than needed.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:508`

## Problem
_idleConnections maps a key to a ConcurrentQueue<PooledConnection> (:301-302); returns Enqueue at the tail (:595) and acquisition TryDequeues from the head (:508), so every acquire takes the least recently used connection. Two effects: (1) each connection idles N times longer between uses (N = idle connections), which is exactly what lets NAT bindings and server keep-alive timers expire; PooledConnection.IsAlive cannot see a silent NAT drop (the class comment says so, :74-77), so the stalest candidate is also the likeliest dead one; (2) a steady trickle of requests round-robins all N connections and keeps each one's LastUsed fresh, so the pool never shrinks to what the load needs. The scavenger re-enqueues survivors in the same order (:885-888).

**Failure scenario.** Mobile client: a burst opens 6 connections, then one idempotent request every 10 s behind a carrier NAT that drops bindings after 30 s of silence. FIFO hands out connections idle for 10, 20, 30, 40 s: the third and fourth requests land on silently dead sockets and each waits the 10 s ReusedConnectionFirstByteTimeout before its retry (a POST fails or waits for the request timeout). With most-recently-used reuse the same traffic always reuses a connection idle for 10 s and the other five expire unused.

## Suggested fix
Reuse most-recently-returned first (a per-key stack, or a deque that takes from the hot end) and let the scavenger evict from the cold end.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Idle connections are reused most-recently-returned first (stack or deque taken from the hot end)
- [ ] The scavenger evicts from the cold end (oldest first)
- [ ] Under steady low concurrency with N idle connections only the hot ones are used and the rest expire by idle timeout
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `net-runtime-08` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/net.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. _idleConnections is ConcurrentDictionary<string, ConcurrentQueue<PooledConnection>> (TcpConnectionPool.cs:301-302); EnqueueConnection appends at the tail (:594-595) and AcquireConnectionWithOwnedPermit takes from the head (:508), so the connection idle longest is always reused first; the scavenger re-enqueues survivors in order (:882-888). Nothing reorders by LastUsed, and no test asserts an order (rg fifo/lifo/oldest over Tests/Runtime/Transport finds nothing). Scenario holds with the defaults: mobile idle timeout 45 s (PlatformConfig.cs:60-63), so after a 6-connection burst and one request per 10 s the pool hands out sockets idle 10/20/30/40 s; IsAlive cannot see a silent NAT drop (:73-77) and the only recovery is the 10 s first-byte watchdog, armed for idempotent replayable requests only (RawSocketTransport.cs:344-354). Each reuse also refreshes LastUsed (:522, :590), so a trickle keeps about idleTimeout/period connections alive instead of one. No open issue tracks it (#364 is the retry's lease choice, not the idle order).

title: [Transport] SAEA, PollSelect, proxy/CONNECT and NAT64 code is statically reachable in every build because selection uses enum switches in always-used types
body:
## Summary
Stream creation chooses SAEA, PollSelect or proxy paths through enum switches and inline branches inside TcpConnectionPool and related types. The linker sees every implementation as reachable, so unused ones cannot be stripped. This enlarges player builds that need only one mode.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:661`

## Problem
TcpConnectionPool.CreateConnectionAsync picks the base stream with 'switch (_socketIoMode)' (661-672) that constructs SaeaStream/SaeaSocketChannel and PollSelectStream/PollSelectSocketChannel directly, so the linker keeps both opt-in implementations even when the default NetworkStream mode is the only one used: SaeaSocketChannel 405 + SaeaStream 140 + SaeaCompletionSource 64 + PollSelectSocketChannel 674 + PollSelectStream 136 = 1419 lines, plus a dedicated thread type per PollSelect channel. Nat64AddressSynthesizer (259 lines) is called unconditionally at 649. The proxy feature (about 730 lines in RawSocketTransport.cs:838-1581 plus Http1/ConnectReplyReader.cs, 419 lines) is reached from DispatchAttemptAsync's 'if (proxy != null)' branch (565). SocketIoMode, ProxySettings and HappyEyeballsOptions live in Core, so there is no compile-time define or separate asmdef that removes any of it.

**Failure scenario.** A mobile project that uses only the default socket mode and no proxy (proxies are effectively a desktop/Editor feature: on iOS/Android the HTTP_PROXY variables are not set and the http:// proxy leg is refused by the default cleartext policy) still ships about 2.8k lines of channel, proxy and NAT64 code that no setting of its client can reach.

## Suggested fix
Replace the enum switch with a stream-factory delegate that the mode-specific code registers (or that ConnectionPoolOptions carries), and move proxy dispatch behind an internal IProxyDispatcher created only when a ProxySettings is configured, so unused implementations lose their static reference and the linker can drop them. Scripting defines (TURBOHTTP_NO_PROXY and similar) are the cheaper alternative.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Mode-specific stream creation is registered through a stream-factory delegate (or one carried by ConnectionPoolOptions)
- [ ] Proxy dispatch sits behind an internal IProxyDispatcher created only when ProxySettings is configured
- [ ] A minimal HTTP/1.1 player build no longer references the unused implementations (size or linker report recorded)
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Transport] No shared dial or CONNECT helper: WebSocket.Transport re-implements DNS-with-timeout, connect pipeline and CONNECT handshake, and the copies differ
body:
## Summary
The pool, RawSocketTransport and RawSocketWebSocketTransport each carry their own copy of DNS resolution with timeout, the connect pipeline and the CONNECT tunnel handshake. The copies already differ in behaviour (for example 407 handling and reply parsing), so fixes land in one path only.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:716`

## Problem
TcpConnectionPool.ResolveDnsAsync (716-745) and RawSocketWebSocketTransport.ResolveDnsAsync (Runtime/WebSocket.Transport/RawSocketWebSocketTransport.cs:320-346) are the same code, but the first reports a DNS timeout as UHttpException(Timeout) and the second as TimeoutException. Unwrapping an all-failed Happy Eyeballs race: ConnectWithDeadlineAsync rethrows through ExceptionDispatchInfo (776-790), the WebSocket copy uses 'throw aggregate.InnerExceptions[0]' (314-317), which resets the stack trace. CONNECT: RawSocketTransport.BuildConnectRequest sends 'Connection: keep-alive' (RawSocketTransport.cs:1524-1551) and reconnects when a 407 is not reusable (1268-1278); ProxyTunnelConnector.WriteConnectRequestAsync sends 'Proxy-Connection: Keep-Alive' (Runtime/WebSocket.Transport/ProxyTunnelConnector.cs:139-157) and fails instead (120-127). The WebSocket path always wraps the socket in HoldingNetworkStream (142), so SocketIoMode never applies to it. Both assemblies already share ConnectReplyReader, Nat64AddressSynthesizer and HappyEyeballsConnector through InternalsVisibleTo, so the remaining glue is what is duplicated.

**Failure scenario.** A fix to one dial path (for example the #322 localhost rule, the #167 NAT64 fallback or the #229 407 handling, each of which had to be applied twice) is missed in the other, and the same proxy sees two differently shaped CONNECT requests from one application depending on whether HTTP or WebSocket opened the tunnel.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 Section 9.3.6

## Suggested fix
Add one internal dialer in Transport (resolve with timeout -> NAT64 fallback -> Happy Eyeballs -> base stream) and one internal ConnectTunnel helper (request, 407 policy, reply parsing) and call both from the pool, RawSocketTransport and RawSocketWebSocketTransport; do it together with the assembly merge tracked in #187.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One internal dialer in Transport implements resolve with timeout, NAT64 fallback, Happy Eyeballs and base stream creation
- [ ] One internal ConnectTunnel helper implements request, 407 policy and reply parsing
- [ ] TcpConnectionPool, RawSocketTransport and RawSocketWebSocketTransport call these helpers and the duplicates are removed

title: [Transport] DNS lookups are not coalesced, a timed-out lookup keeps its thread, and the timeout timer is not cancelled on success
body:
## Summary
Each concurrent dial to the same host starts its own DNS lookup. When the timeout wins, the blocking lookup keeps running on its thread. When the lookup wins, the delay task is not cancelled and stays pending until it fires. Bursts to one host can therefore consume many threads and timers.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:724`

## Problem
Every new connection calls Dns.GetHostAddressesAsync(host) (:724) with no in-flight de-duplication or result sharing, so N parallel dials to one host issue N lookups. On Mono/IL2CPP that API runs the blocking resolver call on a thread-pool thread; on a DNS timeout the task is only observed and left running (:728-736), so the thread stays blocked until the OS resolver gives up while the caller retries. On success the Task.Delay(_dnsTimeoutMs, ct) (:725) is never cancelled: its timer and its registration on the request token stay alive for the full 10 s after every new connection.

**Failure scenario.** Wi-Fi with a blackholed DNS server and a retrying client: each attempt parks another pool thread in the resolver for tens of seconds; with the per-host limit of 8/16 and retries, the pool's worker threads are consumed and timers and continuations of the whole app (including the DNS timeouts themselves) are delayed. What would confirm it: a player trace of thread-pool threads during DNS blackholing.

## Suggested fix
Share one in-flight lookup per host among concurrent dials (and bound the number of abandoned lookups), and cancel the delay with a linked source once the lookup wins.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Concurrent dials to one host share a single in-flight lookup
- [ ] The number of abandoned lookups is bounded
- [ ] The timeout delay is cancelled through a linked source when the lookup completes first
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Transport] Per-host permit eviction in TcpConnectionPool has an acknowledged race and cites a phase that does not exist
body:
## Summary
The permit eviction code removes per-host entries without excluding concurrent GetOrAdd for the same key, so a waiter can end up on a semaphore that was removed and a second one is created, exceeding the cap. A comment calls this advisory and points to a planned phase that does not exist.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:839`

## Problem
EvictSemaphoresIfNeeded (814-850) runs on every GetConnectionCoreAsync call (460); above MaxSemaphoreEntries = 1000 keys it removes any semaphore whose CurrentCount equals the maximum. The comment at 839-843 records a KNOWN RACE: a thread that fetched the semaphore through GetOrAdd just before TryRemove keeps using the orphan while later callers create a new one, 'temporarily allowing 2x the per-host limit', and defers the fix to 'Phase 10'. The class summary (267) repeats that the limits are 'advisory under rare eviction races'. The check 'kvp.Value.CurrentCount == _maxConnectionsPerHost' and the removal are not atomic with a concurrent WaitAsync on the same semaphore, so the orphan case is not limited to idle hosts.

**Failure scenario.** A crawler-style client that has touched more than 1000 origin keys issues a burst to one host while another request triggers eviction: the first requests hold permits on the orphaned semaphore, later ones get a fresh semaphore, and the host sees up to twice MaxConnectionsPerHost connections from a client configured to respect a server's per-client connection cap.

## Suggested fix
Evict under a short lock that also covers GetOrAdd for that key, or keep a per-entry lease count and remove only entries with no outstanding references; drop the stale phase reference and the 'advisory' wording once fixed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Eviction is atomic with GetOrAdd for the key (short lock) or uses a per-entry lease count and removes only entries with no outstanding references
- [ ] The stale phase reference and the 'advisory' wording are removed
- [ ] Concurrent acquire/evict never allows more than MaxConnectionsPerHost holders for one key
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [Transport] Check-then-act races between EnqueueConnection and scavenge/evict/Dispose can orphan a live idle connection
body:
## Summary
EnqueueConnection adds a connection to a per-key queue while the scavenger, eviction or Dispose may concurrently remove that queue from the dictionary or finish disposing the pool. The connection is then enqueued in an unreachable queue and its socket is never closed.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:897`

## Problem
EnqueueConnection reads _disposed and IsAlive, then GetOrAdd(key) and Enqueue (:584-595) without any coordination with: the scavenger, which removes the dictionary entry by key when the queue looks empty (:895-898); semaphore eviction, which TryRemoves the queue and drains it (:827-833); Dispose, which drains and clears (:938-945); and a scavenger pass still running after Dispose's 250 ms wait, which re-enqueues survivors (:887). A connection enqueued into a queue that was just removed, or after the drain, is referenced by nothing: never reused, never scavenged, never disposed. Its socket stays open until a finalizer runs; in PollSelect mode the channel's poll thread roots it permanently (thread, socket and two pooled buffers).

**Failure scenario.** High request rate against one host with the idle queue frequently empty: a response completes and calls ReturnToPool exactly as the scavenger sees IsEmpty and removes the entry; the connection lands in the orphaned queue. Over a long session the process leaks one server-side connection per occurrence, and in PollSelect mode one thread each.

## Suggested fix
Remove entries only when the removed queue is still the mapped value and still empty (TryRemove with key and value, then re-check and re-add or drain), and re-check _disposed after the enqueue so a connection that lost the race to Dispose is dequeued and disposed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Queue entries are removed only when the removed queue is still the mapped value and empty (TryRemove with key and value), with re-check and re-add or drain
- [ ] _disposed is re-checked after enqueue and a connection that lost the race to Dispose is dequeued and disposed
- [ ] No connection is leaked in a stress test of enqueue vs scavenge/evict/Dispose
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it
